The hype for the USA vs Japan robot fight got me thinking. Could this type of robot be used militarily in the future? What are some unforseen problems and dangers this could cause? This may seem far-fetched, but the recent rise in drone warfare feels straight out of sci-fi as well.

When drones saw widespread adoption by the US Military, there was barely any legal framework to regulate its use. As a result drone warfare has been characterized by human rights violations, secrecy and ambiguity. As of today, commercial use of drones still faces a legal void. Property of airspace is loosely defined and new privacy concerns remain unresolved. Can a drone trespass property?

I think it would be a good idea to start thinking about potential problems that could arise from human piloted robots. I brainstormed a few ideas to start the conversation:

-What would happen if human-piloted robots were seized or acquired by terrorists states, terrorists groups, insurgencies, warlords or dictatorships? Would the widespread adoption of human-piloted robots by big and small factions even the playing field or deepen imbalances?

-What potential destabilizing effects could this technology have in the world stage?

-What type of warfare do they encourage? Urban or battlefield?

-Could some current technologies become outdated with their introduction? What about army personnel?

-Could their military use start an arms race?

-How should their commercial use be regulated? You can buy Japan's Kuratas right now if you want to.

-Their possible use by police forces: Could they be used to control protests more easily? Patrol the streets? What can civil society do to protect themselves?

I know this is purely speculative, but would love to hear your opinions on the subject. More-so if you are knowledgeable about military technology. I think these robots are effectively "just" a more mobile, lighter tank. But if Metal Gear taught of anything, it's the danger of more mobile, lighter tanks. Discuss!
Are human-piloted robots actually practical? Could they be militarized? What consequences could there be?
We'll have to wait and see. Militarized robots already exist. DHARPA has a bunch of them. It wouldn't be surprising if sooner or later we might see Gudams...

Could this type of robot be used militarily in the future?

Could be sure, but I think a standing/walking robot of this type wouldn't be very practical. They have very high profiles which make them easier targets to hit. I would say we're more likely to develop something smaller and less expensive like micro drones. They're cheaper, easier to mass produce and if I lose one so what. They would easily be able to fly in close undetected, or in a swarm, and attach explosives or explode themselves. They could be small and smart enough to attack critical systems, optics or weapons maybe, so they don't have to destroy or kill in order to disable the mech.

-What would happen if human-piloted robots were seized or acquired by terrorists states, terrorists groups, insurgencies, warlords or dictatorships? Would the widespread adoption of human-piloted robots by big and small factions even the playing field or deepen imbalances?

I'm sure there would be protections against unauthorized people using them. Encrypted pass keys for example. Plus, being a military vehicle it would likely need special training to pilot. I wouldn't consider it a major concern, no more than a tank or any other piece of hardware.

hat potential destabilizing effects could this technology have in the world stage?

Obviously the richer countries will have the edge and the country which develops it first would as well. But like most war machines the opposition will develop their own or change tactics.

Could some current technologies become outdated with their introduction? What about army personnel?

I don't think you'll ever really get rid of the soldier, but the weapons you give him will change. If there are mechs walking the streets they would most likely carry higher caliber weapons with less ammunition. There really isn't a need to suppress a mech.

-Could their military use start an arms race?

We're pretty much already in one. http://www.theroboticschallenge.org/

How should their commercial use be regulated?

An un weaponized mech should probably require some sort of license to operate, like a car or backhoe.

Their possible use by police forces: Could they be used to control protests more easily? Patrol the streets? What can civil society do to protect themselves?

I'd figure them to be too impractical, expensive, and bulky to be the primary means. Sure, they'll probably show up just like the rest of the swat vans, but it would, at best, just be an intimidation tool.

In the 90s I remember the media really focusing on how this album, and rap in general, glorified gang life.

As an adult, the media couldn't have been more wrong. While the album does have songs like, "Gimmie the Loot" where he talks about robbing pregnant women and teenage girls, the album on a whole says very loud and clear, "Gang life sucks".

I mean, he's poor, and he hurts people, and he goes to jail and loses everything. Then he cleans up his act, becomes a successful rapper, gets lots of money, and now people want to hurt him. He realizes how terrible it is to hurt people, he realizes what a bad person he was, he feels guilty for having so much knowing he's a bad person that doesn't deserve any of it, and eventually does right by killing himself at the end of the album.

I often wonder if the media had praised this album instead of trying to villinize it, would "gangsta rap" have been so popular? Like, if the media had focused on Biggies warning instead of the few tracks that were violent... would young kids have grown up generation after generation thinking gangs were cool? I feel like gang and gun violence prevalent in rap today might not be here had everybody heard the real message back in the 90s when it all started.

Pac was no different. A lot of his songs were about how bad it is... drug addiction, babies in trashcans, kids with no fathers, AIDS....

But as a teen in the 90s, I never heard that message. I was too young to figure it out myself, and the media just kept saying, "The guys are gang members"... so I thought that was cool. I thought they were glorifying that life. As an adult, when I listen to these albums, I see now how wrong I was.

Patrick Stump - Soul Punk

When Fall Out Boy were first around, I always thought Patrick Stump was just a whiner who cries out angsty lyrics. Several songs I particularly disliked during the days of FOB were Beat It and Thnks Fr Th Mmrs. Eventually, when FOB went on hiatus, he posted a teaser for a solo album he was working on which impressed me.

That album changed my opinion of him.

Having listened to Soul Punk, I just wish Patrick Stump would ditch Fall Out Boy already and pursue a full solo career. Every song on the album is pretty diverse and I have many favourites from the album, some of which include:

  • Allie - This song has a 70s Soul/Gospel vibe to it. Kinda reminds me of a Motown song which I cannot quite remember.
  • Everybody Wants Somebody - This song goes from sounding like a sports song/parade song to a very, very decent pop-punk song. There's also a nice acoustic version.
  • Dance Miserable - Aside from the message this song is trying to portray about how we should just go along with all the negative things happening in the world, this song is definitive proof that Patrick Stump has a soul voice and has one of the best vocal solos I've heard in the last decade. Dance Miserable also sounds like a Michael Jackson song.
  • Run Dry (X Heart X Fingers) - This track is actually two songs mixed into a single track one after another (Run Dry and Cryptozoology). Run Dry has a really catchy chorus and is about alcoholism and a guy's struggle to control his drinking habits. Meanwhile Cryptozoology has a really nice rhythm guitar riff and a powerful chorus, and has many meanings that can be interpreted from the lyrics.
  • Spotlight (New Regrets) - Interesting fact, Patrick Stump recorded two versions of Spotlight (New Regrets and Oh Nostalgia) and spent months deciding which one to include on Soul Punk. In the end, New Regrets made it and it's the version I prefer for its faster pacing and beat.
